lesson.title: Relational database transactions isolation and indexes
lesson.why: A database can preserve each individual statement while an application still loses updates across a multi-step operation. Transactions, isolation and indexes must be designed together so correctness survives concurrency without making every request scan an entire table.
lesson.what: Relational databases organize rows under constraints and execute transactions with defined visibility rules. Indexes accelerate selected access paths at a write and storage cost. PostgreSQL's isolation behavior must be understood explicitly rather than inferred from generic SQL labels.

concepts.name: Atomicity and constraints
concepts.body: A transaction groups changes so they commit together or roll back. Constraints such as uniqueness and foreign keys protect invariants at the database boundary. Application checks alone can race; a transaction does not automatically enforce a business rule that was never expressed.

concepts.name: Isolation and visibility
concepts.body: PostgreSQL Read Committed normally gives each statement a snapshot of committed data, so two statements in one transaction can observe different concurrent commits. Serializable provides stronger guarantees but can abort transactions that applications must retry as a whole.

concepts.name: Concurrent updates
concepts.body: Reading a value, calculating elsewhere and writing it back can overwrite another update. Atomic SQL updates, row locks or optimistic version checks address different concurrency needs. Keep lock duration bounded and use a consistent acquisition order to reduce deadlock risk.

concepts.name: Index trade-offs
concepts.body: An index can locate selective rows without a full scan, but inserts and updates must maintain it. Column order matters for multicolumn access paths. Use query plans and representative data; an index's existence does not guarantee the planner will choose it.

e2e: Begin a transaction and read or lock the records required by the invariant.
Apply constrained changes with the intended isolation and concurrency mechanism.
Commit the complete unit or roll it back and retry when the contract requires.
Inspect query plans and latency while preserving the same correctness guarantees.

tasks.name: Work an atomic transfer
steps: Offline, accounts hold 100 and 50 units. Transfer 20 by debiting the first and crediting the second in one transaction. Expected committed balances are 80 and 70, total 150. A failure between statements must roll back both changes.

tasks.name: Expose a lost update
steps: Two fictional workers read stock 10 and each writes 9 after a sale. Final 9 loses one decrement; expected stock is 8. Propose an atomic conditional update that decrements only when stock is positive, checking the affected-row count.

tasks.name: Compare snapshots
steps: Transaction A reads a value, B commits a change, then A reads again under Read Committed. The second statement may see B's change. Explain why wrapping both reads in one transaction does not automatically give a fixed transaction-wide snapshot at this level.

tasks.name: Choose an index experiment
tasks.goal: Match an access path to a query.
steps: A fictional orders query filters customer_id and sorts created_at. Propose evaluating an index beginning with customer_id and then created_at. Compare its plan and write cost on representative isolated data rather than adding indexes to every column or claiming a speedup without measurement.

key_terms: Transaction: atomic unit of database work.
Isolation: rules for concurrent transaction visibility.
Constraint: database-enforced data invariant.
Index: auxiliary structure supporting selected access paths.
lesson.safety: Use paper tables only. Do not run migrations, locking experiments or performance tests against a shared database.
cleanup: Retain the synthetic transaction schedule and index hypothesis; no database records or schemas were changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical stock counter loses decrements although each request uses a transaction. What would you inspect?
interview_points: Look for a raceable read-modify-write sequence.
Use atomic updates, constraints or appropriate locking.
Check actual isolation semantics and retry behavior.
Preserve the inventory invariant rather than merely adding BEGIN and COMMIT.

data/relational-database-transactions-is.core: Transactions need explicit invariants and concurrency mechanisms. PostgreSQL Read Committed is statement-snapshot based. Use atomic updates or suitable locking/version checks, and evaluate indexes against real access patterns with their write costs.
objectives: Explain lost updates and transaction isolation.
prerequisites: Understand tables, rows and basic SQL operations.

storyboard.title: Two transactions overwrite the same stock decrement
storyboard.objective: Explain why atomic updates matter beyond transaction wrappers.

scenes.title: Both read ten
scenes.caption: Separate calculations start from the same observed value.
scenes.narration: Both transactions read stock ten and independently calculate nine. A transaction wrapper alone has not serialized their read-modify-write logic.

scenes.title: One decrement disappears
scenes.caption: Writing nine twice does not record two sales.
scenes.narration: Each worker writes its calculated value. Final stock remains nine instead of eight, violating the intended inventory effect.

scenes.title: Use an atomic constrained update
scenes.caption: Let the database coordinate each decrement.
scenes.narration: A conditional atomic decrement and checked row count preserve the stock invariant under concurrency, with appropriate handling when no stock remains.

lesson.title: Database replication partitioning and consistency
lesson.why: Replication and partitioning solve different problems: copies can improve resilience, while splitting data can distribute work. Confusing them leads to stale reads, overloaded partitions and failover plans that cannot safely decide which node may accept writes.
lesson.what: Replication maintains multiple copies of data; partitioning assigns different subsets to different owners. Consistency describes observable ordering and freshness. A design must specify write acknowledgement, read routing and failover behavior under delays or network partitions.

concepts.name: Replication timing
concepts.body: Asynchronous replicas can lag behind committed primary writes. Synchronous acknowledgement can wait for selected replicas, trading latency or availability for stronger durability behavior. Exact guarantees depend on configuration; a replica count alone does not establish zero data loss.

concepts.name: Partition keys
concepts.body: A key determines where data is stored or processed. Evenly distributed keys can spread load, while a popular tenant or timestamp range can create a hot partition. Resharding moves ownership and must handle routing changes, data movement and concurrent writes.

concepts.name: Read consistency
concepts.body: Read-your-writes may require reading the primary or waiting for a replica to reach a known position. A read quorum and write quorum that overlap can be useful, but overlap arithmetic alone does not prove linearizability without a correct versioning and coordination protocol.

concepts.name: Failover authority
concepts.body: Promotion must prevent an old primary from continuing conflicting writes, commonly through fencing and agreed leadership rules. A network partition can leave nodes alive but unable to communicate. Availability decisions must protect the application's consistency requirements, not merely choose any reachable replica.

e2e: Route a write to the correct partition owner or authorized primary.
Acknowledge according to the configured replication and durability contract.
Serve reads from locations that satisfy the requested freshness semantics.
On failure, establish one valid write authority and reconcile lag before resuming the intended traffic.

tasks.name: Calculate replication exposure
tasks.goal: Relate lag to possible recent data loss.
steps: A fictional asynchronous replica trails by four seconds while writes average 25 records per second. Roughly 100 recent records may not have arrived if the primary is lost. Label this an estimate, not a guaranteed bound or an exact loss prediction.

tasks.name: Detect a hot partition
steps: Four partitions hold equal record counts, but one tenant produces 70 percent of requests in a single partition. Explain why equal storage does not imply equal load. Propose measuring key-level demand before changing partition strategy or adding replicas blindly.

tasks.name: Work a quorum intersection
steps: With three replicas, read two and write two, the sets must overlap in at least one member. Demonstrate using {A,B} and {B,C}. State that stale versions, concurrent writes and faulty coordination still require a correct consistency protocol.

tasks.name: Plan safe promotion
steps: A hypothetical primary is unreachable from the controller but still accepts some clients. Require fencing or a documented leadership mechanism before promoting a replica. Decide how lagging data and client retries are handled rather than equating unreachable with certainly dead.

key_terms: Replication: maintaining additional copies.
Partitioning: distributing different data subsets.
Fencing: preventing obsolete authority from writing.
Read-your-writes: visibility of a client's completed writes.
lesson.safety: Use fictional replica sets and workloads. Do not fail over databases, change partitions or interrupt replication.
cleanup: Retain the synthetic authority and routing diagram; no databases or replicas were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical replica is healthy but sometimes returns a value older than the user's successful update. What explains it?
interview_points: Check asynchronous replication lag and read routing.
Define the required read-your-writes contract.
Use primary routing or position-aware waiting where supported.
Do not infer freshness from replica health alone.

data/database-replication-partitioning-a.core: Replication copies data; partitioning divides ownership. Define acknowledgement and read freshness explicitly, measure hot keys and lag, and fence obsolete primaries during failover. Quorum overlap is not a complete consistency proof by itself.
objectives: Distinguish replication, partitioning and consistency requirements.
Reason about lag, quorums and safe write authority.
prerequisites: Understand transactions, replicas and network failures.

storyboard.title: A healthy replica returns an older value
storyboard.objective: Connect asynchronous replication with read-after-write behavior.

scenes.title: Primary acknowledges
scenes.caption: The write is committed before every replica catches up.
scenes.narration: The primary acknowledges an update under an asynchronous replication contract, while its read replica has not yet replayed that change.

scenes.title: Read reaches lagging replica
scenes.caption: Operational health is not freshness evidence.
scenes.narration: The client reads from the healthy but lagging replica and sees the previous value, contradicting an assumed read-your-writes guarantee.

scenes.title: Honor the freshness contract
scenes.caption: Route or wait according to the required visibility.
scenes.narration: The application uses the primary or a supported position-aware wait for this read, while ordinary replica reads retain their documented freshness trade-off.

lesson.title: Redis caching invalidation TTL and stampede prevention
lesson.why: A cache can accelerate reads while returning stale data or overwhelming the database when entries expire together. Correct cache design states which data may be stale, how updates invalidate it and how concurrent misses are controlled.
lesson.what: Redis commonly serves as a low-latency cache with expiring keys and configurable eviction. Cache-aside applications consult Redis, load misses from an authoritative store and populate entries. The source of truth and acceptable staleness must remain explicit.

concepts.name: Cache-aside flow
concepts.body: On a miss, the application reads the authoritative store and writes a cached value. A hit avoids that read but may be stale. If Redis is unavailable, fallback traffic can overload the source, so cache failure needs a capacity-aware degradation plan.

concepts.name: TTL and eviction
concepts.body: TTL limits how long an entry remains eligible before expiration; it is not proof of business freshness during that interval. Memory-pressure eviction can remove entries earlier according to policy. Expiration and eviction are different reasons for a miss and need separate metrics.

concepts.name: Invalidation races
concepts.body: Updating the database and deleting or refreshing a cache entry are usually separate operations. Concurrent readers can repopulate older data during that gap. Versioned values, careful write ordering or stronger coordination may be needed where bounded staleness is insufficient.

concepts.name: Stampede protection
concepts.body: Many simultaneous misses for one hot key can issue duplicate source reads. Request coalescing lets one loader serve waiting callers; TTL jitter spreads unrelated expirations. Locks need ownership, expiry and safe release, and stale serving is acceptable only for explicitly permitted data.

e2e: The application checks a key whose meaning and freshness policy are defined.
On a hit it returns an eligible value; on a miss a bounded loader reads the source.
The loader stores the value with the intended TTL while other requests coalesce or degrade safely.
Writes trigger documented invalidation and metrics distinguish hits, expiration, eviction and source overload.

tasks.name: Calculate remaining TTL
steps: A fictional key is populated at second ten with TTL 30 seconds. At second twenty-five, ordinary remaining TTL is 15 seconds, and expiry is at second forty unless changed or evicted. This does not guarantee the underlying business record stayed unchanged.

tasks.name: Quantify a stampede
steps: One hundred requests miss the same hot key simultaneously. Without coordination they may create 100 source reads; with successful single-flight loading, one read can supply all waiting requests. Account for timeout and loader failure rather than promising perfect coalescing under every condition.

tasks.name: Trace stale repopulation
steps: Offline, reader A loads old data, writer B commits new data and deletes the cache, then A stores its old result. The cache is stale again. Propose version checks or an explicit bounded-staleness policy; deletion alone did not make the sequence atomic.

tasks.name: Design cache failure behavior
steps: A fictional database safely handles 200 reads per second but normal uncached demand would be 1,000. A Redis outage cannot safely fall through without limits. Plan bounded concurrency, load shedding or permitted stale responses, preserving correctness for sensitive data.

key_terms: TTL: time-to-live for a key.
Eviction: removal under memory policy.
Cache-aside: application-managed cache lookup and fill.
Stampede: concurrent misses overwhelming the source.
lesson.safety: Use paper keys and synthetic rates only. Do not connect to Redis, flush databases or cache personal data.
cleanup: Retain the cache timeline and failure policy; no keys, locks or Redis processes were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical database spikes whenever a popular cache key expires. What would you change and verify?
interview_points: Measure concurrent misses and source load.
Coalesce requests for the hot key.
Use bounded waits, jitter and permitted stale serving where appropriate.
Keep freshness, invalidation races and fallback capacity explicit.

data/redis-caching-invalidation-ttl-and-.core: Cache-aside needs an explicit source of truth and staleness contract. TTL expiration differs from memory eviction. Control stampedes and fallback load, and account for races between source updates, invalidation and concurrent fills.
prerequisites: Understand key-value stores, database reads and concurrency.

storyboard.title: One hot-key expiry triggers many source reads
storyboard.objective: Explain request coalescing during a cache stampede.

scenes.title: Cache serves hits
scenes.caption: Most requests avoid a database read.
scenes.narration: The hot key contains an eligible value, so concurrent callers receive it without issuing repeated reads against the authoritative database.

scenes.title: Expiry synchronizes misses
scenes.caption: Many callers attempt the same source read.
scenes.narration: The key expires and a hundred callers miss together. Independent fallback can create a hundred duplicate reads and overwhelm the source.

scenes.title: Coalesce and bound the loader
scenes.caption: One controlled fill serves waiting requests where semantics permit.
scenes.narration: A bounded loader coalesces the shared miss, handles failure explicitly and repopulates the key under the documented freshness policy.

lesson.title: Kafka partitions consumer groups offsets and delivery
lesson.why: Kafka can retain ordered event logs while consumers restart and scale independently. Correct processing depends on partition assignment and offset timing; committing progress before a durable business effect can lose work, while committing afterward can replay it.
lesson.what: Kafka topics contain partitions with ordered records and offsets. Producers choose partitions, brokers replicate logs and consumer groups divide partitions among members. Delivery semantics describe where duplicate or missing effects remain possible across these boundaries.

concepts.name: Partition ordering
concepts.body: Ordering is defined within a partition, not across an entire multi-partition topic. A key commonly influences partition selection so related records stay together. Changing partition counts or partitioning logic can affect key placement and requires consideration of ordering assumptions.

concepts.name: Groups and concurrency
concepts.body: Within a conventional consumer group, a partition is assigned to one active consumer at a time. Additional consumers beyond the partition count may be idle. Different groups can independently read the same topic, maintaining their own progress and application purpose.

concepts.name: Offsets and effects
concepts.body: A committed offset normally identifies the next record to consume. Processing then committing supports replay after a crash and therefore needs idempotent effects. Committing before processing risks skipping work if the consumer fails after saving progress but before the effect.

concepts.name: Replication and transactions
concepts.body: Producer acknowledgements, in-sync replica requirements and broker replication settings affect durability and availability. Kafka transactions can coordinate supported Kafka reads and writes, but exactly-once behavior does not automatically extend to an arbitrary external database, email or payment service.

e2e: The producer appends a keyed record to a selected partition under its acknowledgement policy.
The broker replicates the record according to configured durability requirements.
The group member owning that partition processes the record and durably applies its effect.
It commits the next offset, handling rebalance and crash replay with the sink's actual idempotency contract.

tasks.name: Calculate group parallelism
steps: A topic has four partitions and one conventional group has six consumers. At most four consumers actively own a partition; two may be idle. A second group can independently consume all four partitions without stealing the first group's offset progress.

tasks.name: Commit the next offset
steps: Offline, a consumer successfully processes offsets 0 through 5 and commits 6. Expected resume point is offset 6, not 5 or 7. If the business effect for 5 completed but 6 was never committed, replay may repeat that effect.

tasks.name: Compare crash windows
steps: Draw commit-before-effect and effect-before-commit timelines. The first can lose an effect after a crash; the second can duplicate one. Propose a deduplicated external sink or an appropriate supported transaction boundary rather than claiming an offset setting eliminates every duplicate.

tasks.name: Evaluate an ordering requirement
steps: A fictional account requires deposit and withdrawal events in order. Keep its related events in a partition under a consistent keying policy. Explain why comparing timestamps from different partitions cannot automatically reconstruct a single authoritative total order.

key_terms: Partition: ordered segment of a topic log.
Offset: record position within a partition.
Consumer group: cooperating readers sharing assignments.
ISR: replicas currently considered in sync.
lesson.safety: Use offline logs and offsets only. Do not reset consumer groups, create topics or produce messages to an existing cluster.
cleanup: Retain the fictional offset schedule; no brokers, topics or consumer checkpoints were changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical Kafka consumer writes to an external database and then crashes before committing its offset. What happens on restart?
interview_points: The record can be delivered again.
The external effect needs deduplication or a suitable transaction strategy.
Commit offsets represent the next position.
Kafka transactional guarantees do not automatically cover arbitrary external side effects.

data/kafka-partitions-consumer-groups-of.core: Kafka orders records per partition and assigns partitions within groups. Commit the next offset only with a deliberate effect/replay strategy. Extra consumers cannot exceed partition parallelism, and external sinks need their own idempotency guarantees.
objectives: Explain offset timing and duplicate-effect recovery.
prerequisites: Understand logs, queues, retries and durable writes.

storyboard.title: A completed effect replays after an uncommitted offset
storyboard.objective: Trace the consumer crash window to an external sink.

scenes.title: Effect succeeds
scenes.caption: The external database commits before progress is saved.
scenes.narration: The consumer processes offset five and writes its business effect, but the next offset has not yet been committed.

scenes.title: Consumer crashes
scenes.caption: Replay can repeat an already completed effect.
scenes.narration: The consumer crashes before committing six. Its replacement resumes from older progress and can receive the same record again.

scenes.title: Deduplicate at the effect boundary
scenes.caption: Stable event identity makes replay safe for the sink.
scenes.narration: The sink recognizes the event identifier and returns the existing result, after which the consumer safely records its next offset.

lesson.title: Message queues dead-letter handling and idempotency
lesson.why: A message arriving twice is normal in many durable queue systems. Reliable consumers separate acknowledgement from business completion and treat dead-letter queues as a controlled recovery workflow, not a place where failures disappear from operational responsibility.
lesson.what: Queues buffer work between producers and consumers. Visibility or acknowledgement mechanisms govern retry after failure. Dead-letter handling isolates repeatedly failing messages, while idempotency and transactional effect boundaries protect against duplicate processing.

concepts.name: Delivery and visibility
concepts.body: Receiving a message may hide it temporarily without deleting it. If processing fails or visibility expires, another consumer can receive it. Set and extend visibility according to bounded processing behavior; a long timeout delays recovery, while a short one increases concurrent duplicates.

concepts.name: Acknowledgement order
concepts.body: Acknowledge or delete only after the intended durable effect succeeds. A crash after the effect but before acknowledgement still causes replay. Store a stable message or business-operation identifier with the effect so repeated deliveries do not create repeated charges or records.

concepts.name: Poison messages
concepts.body: Malformed input or an unsupported schema may fail every attempt. Bounded retries and dead-letter routing preserve throughput for valid work. Distinguish permanent validation errors from transient dependency failure rather than repeatedly invoking an operation that cannot become valid by waiting.

concepts.name: Redrive and outbox
concepts.body: Dead-letter redrive needs a diagnosed cause, corrected consumer or data and controlled rate. A transactional outbox can record intended publication alongside a database change, closing one dual-write gap. Dispatch may still repeat, so downstream idempotency remains necessary.

e2e: The producer durably publishes work, or records publication intent through an outbox.
A consumer receives the message under the queue's visibility or acknowledgement contract.
It validates and applies a deduplicated durable effect before acknowledging.
Repeated failures move to a monitored dead-letter workflow with reviewed, rate-limited recovery.

tasks.name: Calculate visibility overlap
steps: A fictional message becomes visible again after 30 seconds, but processing takes 45 seconds without extension. Another worker may start the same work for the final 15 seconds. Set a bounded suitable timeout or heartbeat strategy instead of assuming one delivery.

tasks.name: Work a deduplication table
steps: Message demo-9 requests adding five credits. Starting balance is 20; first committed processing records demo-9 and balance 25 together. A duplicate demo-9 returns the recorded result and leaves 25, rather than adding another five credits.

tasks.name: Classify poison input
steps: A fictional message has an unsupported schema version. Mark repeated identical retries as unlikely to help. Quarantine with a nonsecret error reason and owner, then update the consumer or correct the approved record before considering a controlled redrive.

tasks.name: Plan dead-letter recovery
tasks.goal: Prevent a second incident during redrive.
steps: A dead-letter backlog contains 1,000 messages and the source can safely process ten per second. Ideal drain time is at least 100 seconds before retries or competing work. Start below the known safe rate and monitor failure and duplicate-effect evidence.

key_terms: Visibility timeout: temporary receive exclusivity window.
Acknowledgement: confirmation allowing queue retirement.
Dead-letter queue: holding area for failed messages.
Outbox: transactional record of intended publication.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic message ledgers only. Do not purge queues, redrive real failures or send live purchases, credits or notifications.
cleanup: Retain the mock failure policy; no messages, consumers or queue configuration were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical queue consumer deletes messages before updating the database to avoid duplicates. What failure does that introduce?
interview_points: A crash after deletion can lose the business effect.
Commit a durable idempotent effect before acknowledgement.
Handle replay with stable identifiers and atomic deduplication.
Monitor and recover poison messages through a controlled dead-letter process.

data/message-queues-dead-letter-handling.core: Queue delivery can repeat. Apply durable deduplicated effects before acknowledgement, size visibility for bounded work and distinguish poison inputs from transient failures. Dead-letter queues need ownership, diagnosis and rate-limited redrive.
objectives: Explain visibility and acknowledgement crash windows.
Design idempotent processing and dead-letter recovery.
prerequisites: Understand asynchronous work, retries and database transactions.

storyboard.title: Visibility expires before processing finishes
storyboard.objective: Explain concurrent duplicate delivery and safe effects.

scenes.title: Message received
scenes.caption: Visibility starts, but the business effect is not yet complete.
scenes.narration: The consumer begins processing under a thirty-second visibility window, while its operation needs forty-five seconds in this example.

scenes.title: Duplicate becomes possible
scenes.caption: Another receiver can obtain the message after timeout.
scenes.narration: Visibility expires while processing continues. A second delivery can overlap with the first, so the effect must tolerate concurrent repetition.

scenes.title: Deduplicate and acknowledge
scenes.caption: Commit one effect, then retire the message.
scenes.narration: A stable message identifier and atomic ledger prevent duplicate effects, while the worker adjusts bounded visibility handling and acknowledges only completed work.

lesson.title: Stream versus batch processing and data pipelines
lesson.why: Processing events quickly is useful only when the result remains correct under late arrivals, retries and partial failure. Batch and streaming choices affect latency, state, recovery and operating complexity rather than representing a simple old-versus-new technology preference.
lesson.what: Batch processing operates on a bounded dataset, while stream processing continuously handles arriving records. Pipelines extract, validate, transform and load data with checkpoints and lineage. Event time and processing time differ whenever delivery is delayed.

concepts.name: Latency and completeness
concepts.body: A periodic batch waits for its next run and can produce a complete bounded result. Streaming reduces waiting but must decide when an evolving result is sufficiently complete. Choose the approach from freshness requirements, data volume and correction costs.

concepts.name: Time and windows
concepts.body: Event time records when an event happened; processing time records when the pipeline handles it. Windows group events by a time rule. Watermarks represent progress assumptions about event time, not proof that no earlier event can ever arrive.

concepts.name: State and replay
concepts.body: Aggregations maintain state that must align with source progress. Checkpointing only the input offset but not the corresponding state can lose or duplicate results. Recovery and replay require deterministic transformations or an explicit strategy for nondeterministic external enrichment.

concepts.name: Sink correctness
concepts.body: A pipeline's overall semantics depend on the output system as well as the source and processor. Upserts, stable event identifiers or supported transactional sinks can make replay safe. A processor's exactly-once claim does not automatically extend to arbitrary emails or external API calls.

e2e: Ingest records with stable identity, source position and defined event-time meaning.
Validate and transform data, updating any window or aggregation state.
Write results under the sink's idempotency or transaction contract and checkpoint aligned progress.
Handle late data and replay through explicit correction rules, monitoring freshness and quality together.

tasks.name: Calculate batch waiting
steps: A job runs every five minutes and arrivals are uniform. Average waiting for the next run is about 2.5 minutes, with nearly five minutes worst-case waiting before processing time. State the uniform-arrival assumption rather than treating the average as a service guarantee.

tasks.name: Place a late event
tasks.goal: Distinguish event time from processing time.
steps: An event occurred at 10:04 but arrives at 10:07. In five-minute event-time windows it belongs to 10:00-10:05, not 10:05-10:10. Define whether the earlier result is updated, retracted or marked late according to the pipeline contract.

tasks.name: Check aligned recovery
tasks.goal: Avoid mismatched state and source progress.
steps: A fictional count state equals 100 after source position 100, but only position 90 is restored. Replaying ten records without restoring matching state can yield 110 incorrectly. Require coordinated state/progress checkpoints or idempotent state updates under the chosen framework.

tasks.name: Choose a pipeline architecture
steps: Compare a monthly financial report with a fraud alert requiring seconds-level response. Prefer bounded reconciliation-friendly processing for the report and a suitably reliable stream for alerts, while documenting correction, replay and source-of-truth requirements for both rather than choosing streaming everywhere.

key_terms: Batch: processing of a bounded dataset.
Event time: timestamp of the underlying event.
Watermark: estimate of event-time progress.
Checkpoint: recoverable state and progress record.
lesson.safety: Use paper events and calculations only. Do not replay production streams or publish alerts, payments or reports to real recipients.
cleanup: Retain the fictional window and checkpoint examples; no jobs or external sink records were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical streaming dashboard changes yesterday's totals after recovery. Which time and replay contracts would you inspect?
interview_points: Check event time, late-arrival policy and correction behavior.
Verify state and source-progress checkpoint alignment.
Review sink idempotency under replay.
Distinguish framework guarantees from external side-effect semantics.

data/stream-versus-batch-processing-and-.core: Batch handles bounded data; streams handle ongoing arrival with state and lateness decisions. Define event-time windows, watermark assumptions, aligned checkpoints and replay-safe sinks. Choose complexity from freshness and correction requirements.
objectives: Calculate batch waiting and assign event-time windows.
Explain coordinated state recovery and sink semantics.
prerequisites: Understand events, timestamps, offsets and aggregation.

storyboard.title: A late event belongs to an earlier window
storyboard.objective: Explain event-time corrections in continuous processing.

scenes.title: Window result published
scenes.caption: The processor has an explicit progress assumption.
scenes.narration: The processor publishes a result for the earlier window according to its watermark and permitted lateness contract, not certainty about future arrivals.

scenes.title: Delayed event arrives
scenes.caption: Processing at 10:07 does not change the event's 10:04 time.
scenes.narration: An event from ten-oh-four arrives at ten-oh-seven. Event-time grouping places it in the earlier five-minute window, not the current arrival window.

scenes.title: Apply the documented correction
scenes.caption: Update, retract or record late data according to policy.
scenes.narration: The pipeline follows its late-data policy and writes a replay-safe correction or late record, making the dashboard's revised result understandable and traceable.

lesson.title: Schema evolution data contracts and data quality
lesson.why: A renamed field or changed unit can break downstream consumers even when every message is valid JSON. Data contracts and staged schema evolution preserve meaning across independently deployed producers, consumers and stored historical records.
lesson.what: A data contract defines structure, semantics, ownership and quality expectations. Schema evolution changes that contract over time. Compatibility depends on reader and writer behavior, while quality checks detect missing, invalid, duplicated or unexpectedly delayed data.

concepts.name: Compatibility direction
concepts.body: Backward compatibility commonly means a new reader can process old data, while forward compatibility means an old reader can process new data; precise definitions depend on the serialization system. Test both directions needed during rolling deployment and replay, rather than assuming a new optional field is universally safe.

concepts.name: Meaning and units
concepts.body: A numeric field can retain its type while changing meaning from dollars to cents. Schemas should document units, timezone, null semantics and identifier stability. Structural validation alone cannot detect every semantic change or distinguish an unknown value from a meaningful zero.

concepts.name: Expand and contract
concepts.body: Introduce compatible additions, update producers and consumers with overlap, backfill or translate historical data where required, then retire old fields after verification. Dropping a column or making a new field mandatory before old writers adapt can break otherwise healthy deployments.

concepts.name: Quality and ownership
concepts.body: Check completeness, uniqueness, validity, timeliness and consistency with defined thresholds and owners. Quarantine invalid records without silently discarding their business impact. A quality percentage needs a denominator and time window, and checks should avoid exposing raw personal data in diagnostics.

e2e: Define field structure, business meaning, owners and compatibility requirements.
Introduce an additive or translated contract and test old/new reader-writer combinations.
Validate incoming records and route quality failures to an owned review path.
Measure adoption and historical replay compatibility before removing obsolete fields or rules.

tasks.name: Work a compatibility matrix
steps: A fictional old reader requires amount; a new writer sends only amount_cents. Old-reader/new-writer compatibility fails. Propose temporarily writing both fields with documented conversion while updating readers, and test old stored records with the new reader before retirement.

tasks.name: Calculate a quality metric
steps: In a synthetic batch of 1,000 records, 980 contain a required customer identifier and 20 are missing it. Completeness is 98 percent for this batch and field. This says nothing by itself about identifier validity, uniqueness or all future batches.

tasks.name: Catch a semantic change
steps: Old amount=12.50 means dollars, while new amount=1250 means cents. Both are numeric but differ by a factor of 100. Require explicit units or a new clearly named field and conversion rules; do not let a successful JSON parse serve as migration evidence.

tasks.name: Plan field retirement
steps: Before removing amount, inventory active readers, retained historical records and replay jobs. Confirm adoption and translation coverage using synthetic fixtures. Keep rejected records in a governed quarantine with an owner and nonsecret reason rather than silently dropping them to improve the quality score.

key_terms: Data contract: agreed structure and meaning.
Compatibility: ability of readers and writers to interoperate.
Backfill: populating historical data under a new representation.
Completeness: proportion with required values present.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic records and offline matrices. Do not export personal data, drop columns or rewrite production events.
cleanup: Retain the fictional compatibility matrix and metric denominator; no schemas, records or quality thresholds were changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical event changes amount from dollars to cents without changing its numeric type. Why might existing schema validation miss the break?
interview_points: Structural types do not capture all business semantics.
Document units and conversion rules explicitly.
Use staged compatibility and reader/writer fixtures.
Check historical replay and downstream adoption before removing old fields.

data/schema-evolution-data-contracts-and.core: Data contracts include meaning, units and ownership, not only types. Test required reader/writer compatibility directions and historical replay. Expand, migrate and contract deliberately; report quality with scope and route failures to accountable quarantine.
objectives: Design a staged compatible schema change.
Calculate scoped quality metrics and identify semantic breaks.
prerequisites: Understand structured records, readers/writers and basic data validation.

storyboard.title: A numeric field changes units without changing type
storyboard.objective: Show why semantic contracts matter beyond schema shape.

scenes.title: Numeric validation passes
scenes.caption: Both old and new representations satisfy the primitive type.
scenes.narration: The producer sends a numeric amount. The schema accepts the type but does not establish whether the value means dollars or cents.

scenes.title: Consumer interprets the wrong unit
scenes.caption: The same type can carry an incompatible meaning.
scenes.narration: The older reader treats twelve hundred fifty as dollars instead of cents, producing a hundredfold semantic error despite successful structural validation.

scenes.title: Evolve an explicit contract
scenes.caption: Name units and verify both reader-writer directions.
scenes.narration: The team introduces documented unit-specific fields with staged conversion, tests old and new data paths and retires the old representation only after adoption.
